one_line: User asks to exchange a t-shirt size on an order they assume delivered; it's actually processed, not yet delivered.
User asks to resize sneakers on an order that is actually cancelled and already refunded.
User asks to swap sunglasses lens color on an order that is actually still pending, not delivered.
User asks for a second style change on a t-shirt whose one allowed exchange was just completed this conversation.
User wants a delivered t-shirt exchanged for sneakers -- a different product type, not just a different variant.
User wants a delivered cycling helmet exchanged for sunglasses -- a cross-product-type request.
User (unverified) wants hiking boots exchanged to a specific size-9 variant that is currently out of stock.
User insists on exchanging sunglasses into a variant already confirmed out of stock, willing to wait.
User wants a cycling helmet color exchange charged to a gift card holding only $1, far under the price difference.
User wants hiking boots exchange price difference charged to a $2 gift card despite knowing it won't cover it.
Authenticated user requests a cycling helmet size exchange on an order that actually belongs to a different customer.
User openly asks agent to exchange a cycling helmet on their friend's order, not their own.
Agent laid out a full running-shoes exchange for confirmation; user replies 'I think so' instead of a clear yes.
User wants only one of two identical fleece jackets exchanged now, deciding the second later, risking the one-time limit.
User wants a t-shirt exchange price difference charged to a gift card they don't actually have on file.
User names a real t-shirt item id for exchange, but that item isn't actually part of the order they cite.
User wants two identical t-shirts exchanged but supplies only one new item id to cover both units.
User wants sneakers exchanged to a size/color/material combo that turns out to be out of stock, no item id given.
